entries.title: The Bulls' Bryson Graham makes first two front office hires official
entries.summary: <p>Building out the front office was always priority No. 1 for the Bulls’ new man in charge Bryson Graham and that construction project officially broke ground on Tuesday.</p><p>As multiple reports indicated last week, Stephen Mervis and Acie Law IV were the first two big pieces added to Graham’s front office, as Mervis will serve as the senior vice president of basketball operations and Law will be the vice president of player personnel.</p><p>Keep moving more desks into the second floor of the Advocate Center because Graham is hardly finished.</p><p>Since being named executive vice president of basketball operations earlier this month by team president Michael Reinsdorf, Graham not only promised to advance the Bulls from the days of playing checkers to now start playing chess, but was given an empty checkbook by Reinsdorf to do just that.</p><p>Mervis and Law were just the first two pieces added to the board and smart additions at that.</p><p>Mervis has a nose for salary cap strategy and analytics, spending the last 12 seasons climbing the ranks in Orlando – most recently as their assistant general manager. The strategy background is key, as the Bulls seemingly fell behind on that front during the Arturas Karnisovas regime, according to Reinsdorf.</p><p>As for Law, he spent last season as the director of player personnel for Brooklyn, but prior to that he was with the defending champion Oklahoma City Thunder from 2022-25, serving as the director of amateur scouting.</p><p>It doesn’t hurt that Law and Graham were college teammates back at Texas A&M, but Law’s reputation as a talent finder had taken off in his last few years with the Thunder.</p><p>The immediate focus for both Graham and Law – both considered successful talent evaluators – will be the upcoming June 23-24 NBA Draft, with the Bulls currently holding Nos. 4 and 15 in a loaded class.</p><p>The good news for both men is there’s no catch-up needed because they’ve each been scouting the class for their previous organizations. Graham was with Atlanta, who also acquired a lottery pick from New Orleans, so admittedly had personally scouted all of the top talent the last six months.</p><p>It was a good sign at last week’s draft combine that almost every player projected to go in the top 20 admitted to meeting with Graham and the Bulls.</p><p>But Graham has way more on his plate than just the draft.</p><p>Besides continuing to add to the front office, there’s a little coaching search that will start picking up momentum in the wake of Billy Donovan opting to leave that seat back in April after six seasons.</p><p>There has been a list of names floating out here, including Timberwolves assistant coach Micah Nori and Spurs assistant Sean Sweeney.</p><p>Sweeney was front and center during the double-overtime win by San Antonio in Monday’s Game 1 of the Western Conference Finals, picked up on camera several times giving final instructions to star big man Victor Wembanyama out of timeouts.</p><p>As for Donovan, the initial thought process was the long-time coach would be a shoo-in for the Magic opening, and while he is in the running as the Sun-Times reported, it’s not as clear cut as initially believed, according to a source.</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley

entries.title: Chicago Reader names new publisher
entries.summary: <p>A third-generation Chicagoan from South Shore will be the Chicago Reader's next publisher.</p><p>Malik Jackson, who was previously the executive director and publisher of South Side Media Works, which oversees South Side Weekly and Hyde Park Herald, will join the newsroom June 1, the publication announced Monday.</p><p>"The Reader has a rich and storied history that stands on its own, and I'm thrilled to help usher in a new beginning for the publication," Jackson said in a news release. </p><p>The Reader was founded in 1971 in the Kenwood neighborhood. In 2018, the Chicago Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/6/15/18327975/chicago-reader-sold-to-group-led-by-chicago-crusader-publisher" target="_blank" >sold the Reader</a> to a group led by Dorothy Leavell, the publisher of the Chicago Crusader and Gary Crusader newspapers.</p><p>In recent years, the paper has struggled to stay afloat. </p><p>In 2022, the Reader nearly shuttered during a dispute among board members over the paper's leadership. The dispute, which prevented the paper's transition to nonprofit ownership, centered around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/14/22927012/chicago-reader-future-tracy-baim-board-infighting-nonprofit-leadership" >concerns about then co-publisher and president, Tracy Baim</a>. By the end of 2022, Baim stepped down from her position. </p><p>In January 2025, the publication laid off six employees to reduce costs and prevent closure. Later that year, the Reader was acquired by Noisy Creek, a media company dedicated to alternative weekly publications such as The Stranger in Seattle and the Portland Mercury<i>.</i></p><p>The paper returned to print in February as monthly magazine instead of a weekly newspaper. </p><p>In an editors note announcing the paper's return in February, editor-in-chief Sarah Conway said the Reader was entering a "new era of Chicago journalism."</p><p>Jackson will replace Amber Nettles as publisher. She previously came into the role in 2024, when the publication divided the roles of Solomon Lieberman, who had previously served as both CEO and publisher. In November 2025, she left to join EmpowerLocal as the chief partnerships officer.</p><p><i>Editor's note: A previous version of this story misspelled Malik Jackson's name.</i></p>

entries.title: Arranca la carrera por la primera junta escolar de Chicago completamente electa
entries.summary: <p>LaPamela Williams fue una de las docenas de personas que hicieron fila el lunes por la mañana para presentar las firmas que recopiló para postularse a un asiento en lo que pronto será la junta escolar completamente electa de Chicago.</p><p>Williams, quien es una agente inmobiliaria, se postula para representar el subdistrito 5A en el lado oeste de la ciudad. Esperaba que ser una de las primeras en presentar sus solicitudes de nominación a los funcionarios de la Municipalidad le otorgara un mejor lugar en la boleta de noviembre.</p><p>Es la primera vez que se postula a un cargo. Comentó que ya en sí, el proceso de recolección de firmas ha sido “revelador” porque le permitió evaluar qué temas son los más importantes para sus futuros votantes. Algunas de sus propias prioridades incluyen aumentar la educación financiera y buscar maneras de evitar que los estudiantes falten mucho a la escuela.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Si logro entrar a la junta, puedo aprovecharlo y buscar soluciones prácticas para la comunidad”, dijo Williams.</p><p>Williams fue una de las 50 personas, incluyendo candidatos potenciales, titulares y simpatizantes, que esperaron afuera del Supersitio Electoral de Chicago en el Loop para que abrieran las puertas a las 9 a.m. Al presentar sus solicitudes, se marcó el inicio oficial de las elecciones para la Junta Escolar de Chicago de este año.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-eaa890" name="image-eaa890"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>LaPamela Williams se postula para representar un subdistrito del lado oeste en la Junta Escolar de Chicago. Aumentar la educación financiera y frenar el ausentismo crónico son sus principales prioridades como candidata.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Muchos candidatos dijeron que como parte de sus campañas, planeaban enfocarse en aumentar las calificaciones en lectura y matemáticas de los estudiantes, en asegurarse de que la junta funcione de manera independiente y en mejorar la transparencia financiera del distrito.</p><p>Quien sea elegido también tendrá que abordar los problemas financieros continuos del distrito, la disminución de la inscripción y las investigaciones federales por parte de la administración de Trump. Las agencias federales han amenazado con retener fondos para el distrito y han iniciado investigaciones en las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) por su plan para mejorar los resultados académicos de los estudiantes negros y su política que permite a los estudiantes transgénero usar el baño que se alinea con su identidad de género.</p><p>La Municipalidad celebró sus primeras elecciones para la junta escolar en 2024, pero ese año sólo estaban en juego 10 puestos. Este año, los 20 asientos, así como la posición de presidente de la junta a nivel ciudad, serán decididos por los votantes.</p><p>Los candidatos para la junta escolar deben presentar al menos 500 firmas, mientras que aquellos que se postulan para presidente de la junta necesitan al menos 2,500. Tienen hasta el 26 de mayo para presentar sus solicitudes. Cada candidato en la fila el lunes por la mañana presentó montones de papeles a los funcionarios electorales para confirmar que tenía suficientes firmas.</p><p>Victor Henderson, abogado de juicios que se postula para presidente de la junta escolar, fue la primera persona en cruzar las puertas. Uno de sus organizadores de campaña había estado en la fila desde las 11 p.m. el domingo para asegurar el lugar de Henderson, quien reemplazó al organizador unos 20 minutos antes de que abrieran las entries.title: Gene & Georgetti files breach of contract lawsuit tied to Midway Airport restaurant conflict
entries.summary: <p>The owner of an iconic Chicago steakhouse has filed a breach of contract lawsuit accusing Midway Airport’s master concessionaire of using the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/22/gene-and-georgetti-owner-chicago-midway-airport-bistro-slot-machines" >Gene & Georgetti </a>name to secure an airport contract — only to terminate the agreement to make way for airport slot machines, damaging the restaurant’s brand.</p><p>Michelle Durpetti’s grandfather, Gene Michelotti, founded Gene & Georgetti Restaurant at 500 N. Franklin in 1941 with his partner, Alfredo Federighi, who was nicknamed Georgetti after a famous Italian cyclist. The restaurant is a Chicago institution, one of the city’s oldest steakhouses.</p><p>Durpetti now owns and operates the family-owned business. The restaurant also has a partnership with SSP America, a partner in the consortium that serves as master concessionaire at Midway Airport, to lend its name and brand to the 3,979-square-foot airport restaurant known as Gene’s Bistro.</p><p>In exchange for everything that the Gene & Georgetti brand is known for — from its recipes, menu, tradition and expertise to the look and feel of the Midway restaurant — Gene & Georgetti gets 5% of gross monthly sales.</p><p>Seven months ago, Durpetti was informed by SSP America that Gene’s Bistro would be “closing in the coming months,” and that her 20-year brand license agreement for the eatery was being terminated with 15 years left on the pact. </p><p>The fact that Gene’s Bistro is still open and still paying Gene & Georgetti the monthly fee — without providing sales records — did not discourage Durpetti from taking what she calls her “David vs. Goliath” fight against the concession giant to the next level.</p><p>“They leveraged our reputation, our status, the fact that we’re women-owned — to strengthen that bid and win the bid, then moved on to something better when it appeared,” Durpetti told the Sun-Times Tuesday.</p><p>“I can’t say for sure exactly what it was that appeared. But you and I both know the timing of all of this is a little bit suspect with the casinos and all of those things.”</p><p>Durpetti said she filed a Freedom of Information request with the city's Department of Aviation asking for “all of the information and plans related to the project coming into the space” now occupied by Gene’s Bistro.</p><p>It came back “so heavily redacted, we couldn’t read it.” Durpetti is disputing the need for the redactions, and the document is now in the hands of the Illinois Attorney General’s office, she said.</p><p>“Why are things redacted? Why is there a need to hide something?” she said.</p><p>“The lawsuit itself is not about whether or not a casino goes in… This is about trade secrets, trademark violation. It’s about breach of contract, and it’s about misrepresenting everything that you said you were doing in order to get us to help you win this bid as an anchor brand and then, the minute something better came along, you went ahead and pursued that.”</p><p>The breach of contract lawsuit filed this week in Cook County Circuit Court accuses SSP America of negotiating with Bally’s to turn the Gene’s Bistro space into a sports bar that includes slot machines.</p><p>But that is not the central argument of the restaurant’s lawsuit.</p><p>The complaint accuses SSP of using Gene & Georgetti’s “trademarks, trade secrets” and other of “confidential information” — including recipes, ingredients, suppliers and marketing strategies — only to change the menu in a way that destroys Gene & Georgetti’s reputation and brand.</p><p>“The concept at Midway has Korean tacos on the menu. Would you say that’s conducive to the brand you know is Gene & Georgetti? That’s what we’re talking about,” Durpetti said.</p><p>“My grandfather used to say, you are your name and your reputation. We’ve spent 85 years, three generations building this reputation. SSP in behaving this way puts that reputation at risk. There is not one item on that menu that we create and we served — ever… How is that damage not serious?”</p><p>Officials with SSP America could not be reached for comment on the lawsuit.</p><p>In a statement released to Crain’s Chicago Business, SSP America dismissed Gene & Georgetti’s legal claims as “without merit.” The statement goes on to say that any decision related to the Gene’s Bistro space are “part of a broader evaluation process" and that "no final tenant has been determined."</p><p>Gene & Georgetti has managed to survive economic pressures posed by the pandemic, rising food prices, city mandates and immigration raids.</p><p>The Gene’s Bistro conflict is "a little bit of a David & Goliath tale, but that’s why I’m doing it,” Durpetti said of the lawsuit. “These large concession operators leverage really beloved local restaurants to secure public contracts, and then marginalize them later. I'd like to maybe keep someone from going through what we're going through." </p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: U.S. agrees to drop tax claims against Trump in broadening of IRS lawsuit settlement
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. government will permanently drop tax claims against President Donald Trump, according to a settlement document that is part of a deal to resolve Trump’s $10 billion <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-treasury-irs-tax-records-e3a79e1bfdc94a663504754af80ce183" target="_blank" >lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service</a> over the leak of his tax returns.</p><p>As part of the settlement agreement, the U.S. is “forever barred and precluded” from examining or prosecuting Trump, his sons and the Trump organization’s current tax issues, according to a one-page document posted Tuesday to the Justice Department’s website.</p><p>The settlement, which marks an extraordinary use of executive power, goes beyond resolving litigation and effectively helps shield the president from further examination of his finances and legal conduct.</p><p>The move comes after the Trump administration announced Monday the creation of a nearly <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-doj-fund-irs-trump-family-lawsuit-c9aaa94c59988508c253d7200043cecc" target="_blank" >$1.8 billion fund</a> to compensate allies of the Republican president who believe they have been unjustly investigated and prosecuted, an arrangement that Democrats and government watchdogs derided as “corrupt” and unconstitutional.</p><p>The “Anti-Weaponization Fund” of $1.776 billion will allow people who believe they were targeted for prosecution for political purposes, including by the Biden administration Justice Department, to apply for payouts, creating what acting Attorney General Todd Blanche called “a lawful process for victims of lawfare and weaponization to be heard and seek redress.”</p><p>Blanche, who was questioned by lawmakers Tuesday on Capitol Hill, would not rule out the possibility that people who carried out violence during the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/projects/january-6-cases/" target="_blank" >Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol</a> will be considered for payouts from the new fund.</p><p>Democratic lawmakers and ethics watchdogs slammed the creation of the fund, saying it was corrupt, opaque and had the potential to become a “slush fund” for the president and his allies.</p><p>Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said Democrats intend to “fight every element of this self-dealing settlement.”</p><p>“Not only is this another heinously corrupt act by the most corrupt administration in history, it’s clearly a violation of the law that prohibits interference by executive branch officials in IRS audits.”</p><p>The fund was announced after Trump, his sons Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., and the Trump Organization agreed to drop their lawsuit against the IRS and the Treasury Department. The lawsuit alleged that a leak of confidential tax records caused them reputational and financial harm and negatively affected their public standing, among other allegations.</p><p>According to a separate settlement agreement posted to the Justice Department website Monday, Trump will receive a formal apology from the U.S. government but “will not receive any monetary payment or damages of any kind,” from the settlement.</p><p>Trump told reporters at the White House Monday that the fund is dedicated to “reimbursing people who were horribly treated.”</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson wants an independent watchdog, his inspector general pick says
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Inspector General-designate David Glockner vowed Tuesday to make timely judgments “independent of politics” and focus on improving systems of city government where the “impact is greatest.”</p><p>Before being unanimously backed by the City Council’s Ethics Committee, Glockner said he would not have agreed to become the city’s chief watchdog if he didn’t think Mayor Brandon Johnson was “committed to an effective and independent inspector general’s office.”</p><p>“We‘ve had the conversation. He gave me that assurance … and I accept that assurance,” Glockner told the committee. “If there are times that, despite my best efforts and despite the assurances that have been given, we find ourselves in a spot where there is not cooperation or there are problems, then you’ll hear about it.”</p><p>Glockner would replace Deborah Witzburg, who clashed repeatedly with Johnson and his inner circle over a host of ethics issues and ultimately decided not to seek a reappointment to a second term she was unlikely to get.</p><p>Those issues ranged from the mayor’s decision to deny her investigators access to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/11/04/city-inspector-general-deborah-witzburg-mayor-brandon-johnson-gift-room" target="_blank" >City Hall gift room</a> to the Law Department’s demand to water down ethics reforms and sit in on her interviews with city employees.</p><p>Johnson also rejected Witzburg’s demand that he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/15/city-inspector-general-deborah-witzburg-brandon-johnson-top-adviser-jason-lee-investigation" target="_blank" >fire senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee</a> for refusing to cooperate with her investigation of an alleged quid pro quo threat that Lee made to 34th Ward Ald. Bill Conway in 2023.</p><p>When Glockner acknowledged Tuesday having met with Lee during the appointment process, Conway asked whether the new watchdog had “made any promises to Mr. Lee or anyone else in the administration” about “cases you will investigate or those you will not.”</p><p>“Absolutely not,” Glockner said.</p><p> Glockner refused to comment specifically on Johnson’s refusal to fire Lee. But he stressed that the mayor and his department heads and appointees are “not required to follow” inspector general recommendations.</p><p>“I would be surprised if we are ever at a point where 100% of the OIG’s recommendations are embraced or acted on,” he said. "Decision-makers … are able to take into consideration other facts and other considerations. We don’t dictate what they do.”</p><p>The full City Council must still approve the appointment of Glockner, a former federal prosecutor who helped ComEd dig out of the federal corruption scandal that culminated in the conviction of former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan.</p><p>Glockner used his confirmation hearing to differentiate himself from Witzburg. He said he won’t hesitate to “call balls and strikes,” but he added he plans to try to minimize clashes with the mayor's office by emphasizing “problem-solving over fingerpointing.”</p><p> </p><p></p><p>“A lot of conflict is avoidable. … It’s avoidable by communicating early when you see problems arising. It’s avoidable by building a track record and relationships of trust so that, when you come to somebody with information that’s uncomfortable for them, their first reaction is not, 'you’re out to get me' because they’ve seen you in other settings and they’ve seen you play it straight,” he said.</p><p></p><p>He told alderpersons that two goals would shape his early work.</p><p>The first is to focus the inspector general’s audit work on “areas that matter most” and have the greatest potential to minimize risk, save the cash-strapped city money, or deliver city services more equitably and efficiently.</p><p>The second is to speed the pace of investigations conducted by the inspector general’s office.</p><p>He said investigations “lose value when they take longer than necessary,” and that delays “prolong the time it takes to address problems.” Protracted delays can create “extended clouds” hanging over those who are “unfairly accused.”</p><p>After reading Witzburg’s final quarterly report, Glockner couldn’t help but notice that the percentage of investigations dragging for more than a year have been “creeping up steadily” and is now “north of 60%.”</p><p></p><p>No matter who the mayor or the inspector general is, the relationship between the two almost always ends badly. Glockner is keenly aware of that history, and he said he hopes to avoid repeating it.</p><p>"I'm absolutely sure there will be a time when somebody somewhere is unhappy with the work we've done," Glockner said. "I'm willing to be the voice who sticks up for the facts and pushes."</p>

entries.title: Vocalo, la estación hermana de WBEZ, renueva su programación tras casi cerrar la señal de radio en 2024
entries.summary: <p>Vocalo, la estación de radio musical local que ayudó a convertir a Chance the Rapper y Vic Mensa en raperos de renombre, está lista para lanzar un programa de llamadas en vivo con la esperanza de “dar forma a lo que viene”.</p><p>Vocalo Hotline, un programa semanal que debutará a las 8 p.m. el 29 de mayo tanto en WBEZ 91.5 FM como en Vocalo 91.1 FM, es parte de una importante renovación para la estación musical, que ha tenido dificultades en los últimos años para atraer audiencia y generar suficientes ingresos para cubrir sus gastos.</p><p>“Sabemos que la forma en que las personas interactúan con los programas de radio está cambiando, así que queremos asegurarnos de que nos estamos preparando para seguir recordándole a la gente que tenemos opciones de streaming, un boletín y videos verticales, así como la señal de radio”, dijo Melissa Bell, directora ejecutiva de Chicago Public Media (CPM), la organización matriz de WBEZ, Vocalo y el Chicago Sun-Times. “Sentimos con mucha fuerza que el equipo que tenemos ahora apoya este trabajo, y vale la pena realmente crear un producto que tantas personas en Chicago aman de verdad”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a70000" name="module-a70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El programa de llamadas es parte del renovado enfoque de WBEZ en la programación basada en Chicago, que incluye los programas matutinos “In the Loop” y “Say More”.</p><p>Hotline será una transmisión de radio de una hora construida en torno a las solicitudes de los oyentes, saludos y conversaciones, informó CPM en un comunicado de prensa.</p><p>“El programa está diseñado para cobrar vida también en experiencias digitales, capturando la energía de cada episodio a través de videos, clips en redes sociales, momentos con artistas e interacción en tiempo real con la audiencia”, según el comunicado de prensa. “Cada episodio presentará una mezcla curada de géneros que abarca pop, hip-hop, R&B, house, dance y música independiente, junto con entrevistas de artistas, talento local emergente y un resumen de eventos culturales en Chicago”.</p><p>La DJ de Vocalo, Nudia Hernández, será la anfitriona del nuevo programa.</p><p>Hernández, quien ha estado en la estación durante cuatro años, creció escuchando programas de dedicatorias nocturnos; espera replicar eso aquí, pero con un “factor hiperlocal”.</p><p>“Como alguien que llame acerca de alguien que vio en el autobús 29 en State y Lake,” dijo Hernández como ejemplo. “Quiero poder hacerle a la gente la pregunta: Si pudieras dedicarle cualquier canción a una persona, ¿cuál sería?”.</p><p>¿Y si alguien llama a la “Alternativa urbana” de Chicago y pide a Taylor Swift?.</p><p>“Si alguien está teniendo un mal día y quiere escuchar a Taylor Swift, bueno, ¿sabes qué?, vamos a tocar a Taylor Swift”, comentó Hernández.</p><p>El programa casi no se llevó a cabo.</p><p>Hace dos años, enfrentando una situación financiera cada vez peor, CPM anunció planes para descontinuar las transmisiones de Vocalo, como parte de una serie más amplia de recortes en la organización de noticias.</p><p>“Lanzado por primera vez en 2007, la audiencia de radio de Vocalo no ha crecido, alcanzando solo 11,000 oyentes semanales, con la estación de transmisión operando con pérdidas financieras significativas durante muchos años. Como resultado, la transmisión de música de radio se eliminará gradualmente para el 1 de mayo”, dijo el entonces director ejecutivo de CPM, Matt Moog, al anunciar los recortes.</p><p>Pero la estación de radio no fue sacada del aire.</p><p>“Hubo reportajes en la prensa que aparecieron en 2024 diciendo que Vocalo estaba cerrando, y eso era incorrecto. Estaban considerando cerrar la señal de [radio], pero nunca lo hicimos, y decidimos no hacerlo,” dijo Bell.</p><p>Aun así, el personal de Vocalo se redujo de cinco a dos, quedando sólo Hernández y Morgan Ciocca, quien escribe el boletín semanal en línea de la estación.</p><p>Vocalo tiene alrededor de 15,200 oyentes semanales, según Ariel Van Cleave, directora administrativa de audio de WBEZ. El boletín tiene aproximadamente 34,000 suscriptores.</p><p>El nuevo programa es posible en parte gracias a una subvención de la Fundación John D. y Catherine T. MacArthur, según CPM.</p><p>“La subvención está haciendo posible dar más vida a esta marca y toda la búsqueda musical que siempre ha sido una gran parte de lo que es Vocalo”, dijo Van Cleave.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong fined $5,000 for fan interaction
entries.summary: <p>Major League Baseball has fined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> outfielder Pete Crow-Armstrong $5,000 for “comments made to a fan” at Sunday’s Cubs-White Sox game, according to industry sources.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has the right to appeal, but that determination had not yet been made.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong responded to a female spectator who began to boo him and yell, “You suck” when he was just feet away after just missing a potential highlight reel catch. Crow-Armstrong responded with a profane response; he apologized for his choice of words before Monday’s game here.</p><p>“I’m just bummed out about the word choice and that a bunch of little kids probably find their way to social media and see that as well,’’ he said.</p><p><b>Doing triple-time</b></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Some context on Sunday’s walkoff home run allowed by Cubs reliever Ryan Rolison to Edgar Quero in the 10th inning of the team’s 9-8 loss to the White Sox. Rolison was pitching for the third straight day, appearing in all three games against the White Sox. It was the first time this season Cubs manager Craig Counsell had used any reliever on three successive days.</p><p></p><p>Rolison had pitched on back-to-back days only once previously this season. Last season, his first in the big leagues, Rolison went back-to-back five times in 31 appearances for the Rockies. He had not pitched in three straight games at any time in his professional career.</p><p></p><p>Counsell has turned to Rolison this season in more high-leverage situations, a new role for the left-handed reliever, because of the injuries that had decimated the Cubs pen. Last season with the Rockies, Rolison did not enter once in a game in which the Rockies were ahead. The team went 2-29 in games in which he pitched.</p><p></p><p>This season, the Cubs are 8-3 when Rolison has pitched. He has been credited with wins in three games, the first time when the Cubs scored six runs in the last three innings for a 6-4 win over the Dodgers in L.A April 24, then wins in back-to-back games against the Reds in Wrigley Field.</p><p></p><p>Rolison pitched a third of an inning in Friday night’s 10-5 Cubs win, giving up a home run to Miguel Vargas. He threw 10 pitches. The next night, an 8-3 loss to the Sox, Rolison pitched a scoreless eighth, throwing a dozen pitches. After the game, he said, pitching coach Tommy Hottovy asked him if he could go the next day if needed.</p><p></p><p>“So I stayed late and got a lot of recovery in, and told him I’d tell them how I felt at the throwing program, and I felt good enough to give them an inning or whatever they needed. I was ready to take the ball and help the team win.</p><p></p><p>“…I don’t think the [three consecutive days] had any effect on my stuff. My velocity was good for the two pitches I threw, and I had conviction on the [home run] pitch. [Quero] put a good swing on it.’’</p><p></p><p>Rolison got his chance when left-handed reliever Caleb Thielbar, who won two games and saved two others while picking up for injured closer Daniel Palencia, also went down with an injury, a left hamstring strain.</p><p></p><p>The 39-year-old Thielbar, who had missed 23 games, was activated Tuesday. To make room for him on the roster, the Cubs designated left-handed reliever Ty Blach for assignment.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p><b>“Juuusssst a bit outside”</b></p><p></p><p>According to Umpire Scorecards, the 12 challenged ball-strike calls on ABS Sunday at Rate Field tied the single-season high in MLB this season, and so did the 9 overturned calls. The plate umpire was Chris Segal.</p><p><b>Beauty in the eye of the beholder</b></p><p></p><p>Score one for the Milwaukee Brewers’ social media team. After the Brewers’ 9-3 win here Monday night, they posted a photo of the Brew Crew doing their victory lap, with the caption: “This win is dedicated to the beautiful city of Green Bay.’’</p><p>A segment of the Wrigley crowd Monday night had aimed a disparaging chant at Green Bay, imitating the one chant that achieved consensus over the weekend at Rate Field.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" entries.title: Popular retailer Reformation expands to Lake View and Fulton Market
entries.summary: <p>Retailer Reformation expanded its Chicago presence with two new stores. </p><p>The women's brand, aimed primarily at Gen Z and millennials, opened in Lake View, 3452 Southport Ave., and Fulton Market, 833 W. Randolph St. — neighborhoods that have become a hotspot for trendy retailers. Previously, Reformation's only Chicago store was in Streeterville, which opened in 2019 at 56 E. Walton St. An Oak Brook store opened in 2022.</p><p>The cult brand bills itself as a sustainable fashion label and sells accessories and clothing ranging in price from $38 for a basic tank top to $398 for a silk dress.</p><p>Its new Southport Avenue location was previously home to footwear brand Dr. Martens. Reformation joins other brands in the area like Abercrombie & Fitch, Lululemon, Athletica, Madewell, Gap and Sephora.  </p><p>The new location was “designed with a multi-generational appeal in mind” and a focus on "occasion dressing," according to a news release.</p><p>Reformation's Fulton Market store replaces an Allbirds. The retailer said in a news release that the store's merchandise will cater to a "desk-to-dinner lifestyle."</p><p>Reformation's Chicago stores are in community areas with the highest number of new business licenses, according to city data compiled by Crosstown LA. Between Jan. 1, 2020 and May 18, 2026, Near North Side, which includes Streeterville, saw the third highest number of licenses for retail, personal care and general services out of Chicago's 77 community areas. The Near West Side, which includes Fulton Market, had the fourth highest number of licenses, and Lake View had the sixth highest.</p><p>The new stores incorporate the brand’s tech-focused concept called Retail X, which started in 2017. One of each item is on the shop's floor, and touchscreens and QR codes are displayed so customers can request their size to be added into a dressing room. Each fitting room also has a touchscreen so shoppers can request additional items and sizes. </p><p>Founded in 2009, the Vernon, California-based company started with one store that re-tailored vintage clothing and expanded online in 2013. Reformation now has 58 stores in the United States and 10 internationally. </p><p>It touts “eco-friendly business practices” and releases an annual sustainability report. The brand’s products have been deemed climate neutral since 2015, and the business has been Climate Neutral Certified since 2021, according to a news release.</p><p>Customers are encouraged to recycle their used Reformation pieces through the company’s recycling program, which offers credit toward future purchases.</p>

entries.title: White Sox’ swing-dancing outfielder Tristan Peters finding his groove at the plate
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Tristan Peters has always been light on his feet in the field.</p><p>A center fielder by trade and a swing dancer by hobby, the 26-year-old rookie’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/12/white-sox-tristan-peters-rays-southern-illinois-pete-crow-armstrong-jump-outfielders-statcast" target="_blank" ><u>smooth moves</u></a> and solid glove have entrenched him in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> outfield in desperate need of stability.</p><p>Now Peters looks like he might be finding his stride in the batter’s box to boot, further burnishing his emergence as the type of potential diamond in the rough that’s crucial to any MLB rebuild.</p><p>The former Savannah Banana flashed both sides of his game in the Sox’ series opener in Seattle, making a sprinting catch against the left-field wall at T-Mobile Park, and socking the second home run of his career in as many games.</p><p>If Peters didn’t win over fans with his walk-off single <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-blue-jays-jerry-reinsdorf-home-opener" target="_blank" ><u>in the Sox’ home opener</u></a> against the Blue Jays, he did when he wrote himself into Crosstown lore Sunday with a go-ahead three-run homer over the Cubs en route to their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/white-sox-edgar-quero-tristan-peters-upstage-cubs-everyone-else-in-wild-9-8-bash" target="_blank" ><u>wild series win</u></a>.</p><p>His followup bomb against the Mariners capped a .274/.338/.425 stretch over 30 games with three doubles and 11 RBI.</p><p>“I feel locked in,” Peters said. “I feel like my swing's in a really good spot. I've been hitting the ball hard, some right at people in the last few games, but I think I think it's clicking.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tristan Peters got all of that one 💥⚾️ <a href="https://t.co/MPX7G5qSzk">pic.twitter.com/MPX7G5qSzk</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2056582017802985944?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>There’s nothing flashy about Peters’ .686 OPS in 44 games this season, but the Sox will settle for decent in an outfield riddled by injuries to veteran Austin Hays and Everson Pereira — like Peters, another Rays castoff who had shown <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/21/everson-pereira-white-sox-outfield" target="_blank" ><u>early promise</u></a>.</p><p>Meanwhile, Luisangel Acuna — the Sox’ initial presumptive replacement for Luis Robert Jr. in center — has floundered to a .174/.234/.186 while learning the position.</p><p>The modest but steady production for Peters is all about timing and rhythm, according to manager Will Venable, just like it is for any good dancer.</p><p>“He’s taking really good swings, he’s making good swing decisions, putting himself on time,” Venable said. “[Hitting coach Derek Shomon] and the hitting guys talk about taking your best bat speed to good pitches over the heart of the plate, and he’s done a really nice job embracing that approach, and he’s putting it into action.”</p><p>While Venable also counts Peters as one of his most reliable bunters, the second-year manager said he’s not surprised to see the power arrive.</p><p>“[There have been] some of these early-count swings that he's had that look like he's going to do damage, and then ends up battling, maybe missing the pitch, battling, and then, two-strike approach, puts the ball in play,” Venable said. “But he's hit some balls hard and he has that club in the bag.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Manitoba native whose winding baseball road included stops at Southern Illinois University and Chandler-Gilbert Community College in Arizona, where his line-dancing skills caught the eye of his future partner as well as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/02/white-sox-savannah-bananas-tristan-peters" target="_blank" ><u>the Bananas</u></a>. Peters briefly played for an early iteration of the wildly popular dancing baseball franchise.</p><p>“I've been a lot of places,” Peters said after his Crosstown heroics. “I've experienced a lot of things. It's a lot of learning too, learning things about myself. I met my wife in Arizona, of all places. I never expected to be there, coming from Canada.”</p><p>He let go of expectations after going hitless in his first 12 big-league at-bats with the Rays last season, before the Sox acquired him for cash in the offseason.</p><p>“Just kind of surrendering control is a huge thing, and I think that helps,” Peters said. “Obviously, I'm thinking about those 12 at-bats throughout that whole offseason, but I'm glad I could get more here.</p><p>“It's just like pressing forward every day. You’ve got to know you're not going to be perfect. entries.title: Judge orders release of CPS student's mother from ICE detention
entries.summary: <p>The mother of an 18-year-old Mather High School student was ordered released from immigration custody by a federal judge on Tuesday, though the teen remains detained, according to the family’s lawyers.</p><p>Ricardo Navarrete and his mother, Liliana Navarrete, were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/17/after-mather-student-and-mom-detained-by-ice-a-school-and-soccer-community-are-left-reeling" target="_blank" >detained by federal agents in March</a> during a routine court hearing for their asylum case. The pair arrived in Chicago in 2022 as asylum seekers from Colombia.</p><p>Liliana Navarette was one of 18 people released on a <a class="Link" href="https://joannaklonsky.us3.list-manage.com/track/click?u=5d5e50872dd1af3b8172cf48b&id=674152938f&e=a34e5536a9" target="_blank" >writ of habeas corpus</a> by a U.S. District judge in Kentucky after being held for too long without a bond hearing, according to a statement from her lawyers. The fight for her immigration case will continue in the courts as she returns to Chicago.</p><p>The teen, who has previously described being held in cramped rooms with dozens of men, remains in custody.</p><p>“Liliana can return to her home in Chicago, Illinois and continue to pursue her case before the Chicago immigration court,” Kelli Fennell, an attorney representing the family, said in a statement. “His family and community are hopeful they will soon receive a positive decision in his pending habeas."</p><p>A standout soccer player, Ricardo <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DU83cLsklx4/?img_index=2" target="_blank" >signed to play</a> for community-college soccer powerhouse Truman College after graduating. Those plans are uncertain given his ongoing detention.</p><p>Kristy Morrow, a family friend who has been helping to support the family, had hope for Liliana’s case since her Kentucky court district has been granting habeas petitions. </p><p>Morrow hopes Ricardo’s habeas petition also may be granted following a federal appeals court ruling last week. The ruling says immigration detainees cannot be held without a bail hearing.</p><p>Ricardo has told family he is being kept in a county jail with 90 other men. The lights stay on through the night and there is constant sound, Morrow said.</p><p>“We have a boy missing prom, graduation and his final soccer season," Morrow said. "We need to get this boy home.”</p><p>Richardo will miss the rest of his soccer club's season, which ends Saturday, long before his next court date in July.</p><p>But the team has kept him on the roster. Morrow said. And his name is read out every game by the referee.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/17/after-mather-student-and-mom-detained-by-ice-a-school-and-soccer-community-are-left-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Supporters rallied last month for Ricardo and his mother</u></a>, calling for their release and an end to the Trump administration’s deportation campaign since the end of Operation Midway Blitz in the Chicago area.</p><p>“They’re all seniors, so it’s bittersweet,” she said. “They’ve had a great season, but they realize what’s happening and the gravity of this. Their teammate is missing."</p><p><i>Contributing: Emmanuel Camarillo</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago man charged with DUI in fatal crash that killed Wheaton man on Eisenhower Expressway
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man has been charged with DUI after a fatal accident early Sunday on the Eisenhower Expressway that killed a man and injured at least six others, including himself, on the Near West Side. </p><p>Jose F. Perez Marin, 21, faces three charges of felony aggravated DUI with enhancements because a person was killed and because he didn’t have a valid license at the time of the crash, Illinois State Police said in a statement.</p><p>Perez Marin allegedly rear-ended a Toyota SUV with his GMC SUV around 3 a.m. on westbound I-290 westbound just west of Ashland Avenue, state police said. It allegedly caused the vehicles to hit two others, which also then crashed.</p><p>Benjamin M. Farraday, the 25-year-old Wheaton resident driving the Toyota, was taken to a nearby hospital where he later died, police said.</p><p>Perez Marin is being held in custody as he awaits trial, state police said.</p>

entries.title: Live Nation sued for negligence in alleged sexual assault of minor at Credit Union 1 Amphitheatre
entries.summary: <p>Live Nation Entertainment is being sued for negligence after a man allegedly assaulted an intoxicated 16-year-old girl at a Wiz Khalifa and Seal Paul concert last year in southwest suburban Tinley Park.</p><p>In a news conference Tuesday in the Loop, attorney Molly Wells said Live Nation failed to uphold its security duties during the concert as the girl was sexually assaulted in an area that was meant to be closed off. The suit also alleges the venue failed to ensure that alcohol would not be provided to or consumed by minors.</p><p>“The restricted area was open. The cameras weren’t being watched. A minor was given alcohol,” Wells said. “Those are violations that Live Nation allowed to happen and actively participated in.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Live Nation said in a statement they "cooperated fully" with law enforcement in the case.</p><p>"The safety and security of our guests is our top priority," the company said in the statement. "As this matter involves ongoing litigation, we do not have anything further to share at this time."</p><p>The minor, identified in the lawsuit under the pseudonym Jane Doe, attended the concert at Credit Union 1 Amphitheatre on July 22, 2025, when Roman Basso allegedly followed her while going to the bathroom, according to the suit, filed Tuesday in Cook County Circuit Court.</p><p>Basso led the girl to a restricted, enclosed area, where he allegedly sexually assaulted her, the suit states. Basso was later charged with aggravated criminal sexual assault and bodily harm in February, according to the complaint. Basso's case is ongoing.</p><p>The then-16-year-old from Cincinnati, Ohio, was intoxicated during the sexual assault after being given alcohol that her friend's mother purchased from vendors at the venue, according to the lawsuit, which seeks $150,000 in damages .</p><p></p><p></p><p>This case is not just about one family, Wells said. </p><p>“Concert season is coming. And many of those venues are run by Live Nation. These parents deserve to know that the company that is taking their money is taking care of the children that are coming to their venue," Wells said.</p><p>Live Nation has a history of major security incidents at its events, the suit alleges.</p><p>In 2017, Live Nation promoted an Ariana Grande concert during which 22 people were killed after a suicide bomber carried out an attack outside the Manchester, England, venue. Later that same year, Live Nation promoted a Jason Aldean concert in Las Vegas where 60 people were killed and about 867 people were injured in a mass shooting.</p><p>The Astroworld Festival in 2021 in Houston, where 10 people died after a crowd rushed to the stage, was also hosted by Live Nation.</p><p>Wells told the Chicago Sun-Times that parents should be proactive when sending their children to Live Nation events, but the company still has the legal responsibility to follow security protocol.</p><p>“Ask whether that venue has adequate security. Ask whether they actually restrict areas that are supposed to be restricted," Wells said. </p><p></p>

entries.title: Former high-ranking Chicago cop sues city, claims he was wrongfully placed on 'don't hire' list
entries.summary: <p>A former high-ranking Chicago cop has sued the city, Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling and others alleging he was added to the city's do-not-hire list based on bogus information about his disciplinary record.</p><p>Michael Barz, who rose to the rank of deputy chief, filed the defamation lawsuit last month in federal court in Chicago, claiming the move tarnished his reputation and contributed to the "loss of the professional dignity earned through nearly thirty years of decorated service."</p><p>The lawsuit highlights a memo sent to Snelling on April 26, 2025, by Joy Brown, another defendant in the case who serves as director of human resources for the city's Office of Public Safety Administration. The memo recommended that Barz be added to the do-not-hire list, focusing on two disciplinary investigations that purportedly led to recommendations for 15-day suspensions. </p><p>However, Barz never faced a sustained disciplinary complaint over his career, including in those two cases, the suit holds. And those suspensions weren't imposed.</p><p>Still, Snelling signed the memo less than a week later — on April 30, 2025 — placing Barz on the do-not-hire list and noting he was "retiring in lieu of discharge for misconduct," according to the lawsuit. But that same day, Snelling signed an "irreconcilable" form saying Barz was in good standing and was "eligible for retirement credentials."</p><p>By May 27, 2025, the city's Department of Human Resources formally prohibited Barz from being rehired by the police department and noted in his personnel file that he had retired instead of being fired, the lawsuit states. </p><p>Barz sought to be removed from the do-not-hire list that September, submitting his disciplinary record showing he had never been the subject of an investigation with sustained findings, according to the suit. His appeal was initially denied, but the decision was later reversed on April 15 after Barz's attorney got involved. The lawsuit was filed April 24.</p><p>Human Resources Commissioner Sandra Blakemore, who is also named as a defendant in the lawsuit, acknowledged that same month that the police department's Bureau of Internal Affairs "had provided inaccurate information" about Barz's disciplinary history and formally requested that he be removed from the do-not-hire list. Barz previously worked as an internal affairs investigator.</p><p>Barz is seeking compensatory damages, an order to correct his personnel record to show he retired in good standing and for the city to stop sharing the do-not-hire memo in response to public records requests.</p><p>John Garrido, one of Barz's attorneys, said the lawsuit "speaks for itself and we will try this case in court."</p><p>A spokesperson for Chicago's Law Department said the city hadn't been served with the lawsuit and declined to comment on the pending litigation.</p><p>Barz was recently at the center of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/10/16/chicago-police-cpd-franklin-paz-michael-barz-traffic-stop-misconduct-lawsuit-settlement" target="_blank" >whistleblower lawsuit</a> that was settled for nearly $1 million, although he wasn't named as a defendant. </p><p>Lt. Franklin Paz Jr. alleged that Barz pushed an illegal traffic stop quota as deputy chief of the Community Safety Team, a specialized unit championed by former police Supt. David Brown. City Hall's former inspector general later pushed to have Brown <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2024/07/17/chicago-top-watchdog-ex-police-supt-david-brown-do-not-hire-list" target="_blank" >added to the do-not-hire list</a> after he refused to cooperate with an investigation stemming from a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/2/22/22946554/cpd-yolada-talley-police-department-internal-affaris-chief-niece-heroin-lexus" target="_blank" >drug bust involving a police chief’s car</a>.</p><p>Barz previously told the Chicago Sun-Times that the allegations in the lawsuit "were never proven true."</p><p>He was reassigned from deputy chief to commander and ultimately retired in 2025 as a captain.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2024/07/17/chicago-top-watchdog-ex-police-supt-david-brown-do-not-hire-list" target="_blank" >Chicago’s top watchdog pushed to add ex-Police Supt. David Brown to city’s do-not-hire list</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/16/chicago-police-cpd-joseph-vecchio-misconduct-discipline-complaints-lawsuit-snelling-traffic-stop" target="_blank" >Top cop benches Chicago police officer who racked up the most complaints in recent years</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2015/3/25/18593280/cop-says-she-was-told-arrest-could-go-away-if-she-dropped-federal-lawsuit" target="_blank" >Cop says she was told arrest could ‘go away’ if she dropped federal lawsuit</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
